segment:
She let go. They both gave a little smile and started to shuffle awkwardly in separate directions. “I’ll show you the—” Mara began.
He was already heading back to the couch, one hand lifted in a gesture of invitation. “Sorry,” he said over his shoulder. “I was just… hanging out here. Enjoying a view.”
She walked over to sit down across from him on the other side of the low table. He looked at her with a grin, as if she were funny.
“Hello again,” he repeated when she didn’t say anything right away.
She raised an eyebrow and returned his smile. “And I thought you’d been looking at me.”
He laughed. “Maybe you’re not quite as fascinating as you think.”
They both smiled, but now there was a slight awkwardness in the air. He looked around for something to say and decided to comment on her choice of clothing: “Nice jeans,” he said approvingly.
Mara gave him a blank look. “Uh… thanks,” she muttered uncomfortably; then quickly added with more enthusiasm than was probably necessary, “I like those shorts.”
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

The two pairs of eyes held each other through an entire exhale.
And then the young man had pushed himself up on the armrests, stretched to his full height, and strolled over to shake her hand.
“Mara?”
He was closer than she would have guessed from where he’d been sitting, broad-shouldered and strong-chinned in a white T-shirt, grinning at her through dark-framed glasses as he reached out for the handshake. She took it.
“Jonah,” he said.
“Hello,” she replied, and then they stood there, still shaking hands, not knowing what to do next.

segment:
Jonah seemed to recover first; he dropped her hand and gestured with a flourish toward the rest of the common room.

“This is where all the magic happens,” he declared.
She blinked. “I see,” she managed to say. “And you’ve already—?”
“What? Been here? No,” he said, “not quite.” He grinned again. “It’s my first time too.”
So they were two newcomers then, together but still strangers. She hoped that the tension in her jaw and the blank look on her face would be temporary, until she could figure out how to begin.
Jonah tilted his head a little closer and murmured, “This feels pretty weird, doesn’t it?”

The sudden proximity startled her a little—she stepped back as he bent forward—and the words surprised her as well, because this wasn’t what she’d expected at all. Jonah didn’t seem the type to admit to feeling anything out of the ordinary, even if that was exactly how she had been feeling herself.

segment:
There was only one other guest in the common room, now that Jonah had gotten off the couch, so Mara figured he probably meant to sit at the table with her. But she wasn’t certain, and he didn’t move.
“You’re not from around here,” he offered, reading her tag.
“No, I’m not.”
She tried again for the name she had seen on his badge, but it still wasn’t coming; her attention must have focused on his face and left the lanyard entirely out of frame. “What did you say your last name was?”
He smiled again.
“Reed. Jonah Reed.”

Prose movement 1
A burst of voices sounded behind Mara and she turned away from Jonah as someone pushed open the door into the common room. The new arrivals all had names and positions printed on badges like hers and Jonah’s: they were fellow guests, come home from dinner.

segment:
Prose movement
But it didn't take long: there was a quiet pause, a rustle of fabric and the murmur of a second voice, and then Adrian himself stepped through the door followed by two older visitors, a couple from somewhere on the East Coast.

"Ah, there you are, Mara. Jonah, I believe you've met. And these are our friends Dr. and Mrs. Levine. They were just telling me about their latest trip to France..."

The guests flowed in like ripples spreading out from Adrian's voice. Mara took in the scene, noticing how Adrian seemed to effortlessly orchestrate the space, drawing attention to himself before turning it subtly toward others. He was skilled at making everyone feel included, even as he maintained control of the conversation.

segment:
“Good to meet you,” she finished. “I’m Mara.”
He smiled. “Yeah, I got that part.”
They let go and started at each other.
He had a voice like summer rain on the roof of a cabin in the mountains, soft and warm and a little lazy. But he wasn’t lazy at all; Mara could feel it. The way he held himself, the way he moved. Even the way he grinned, a little crooked and a lot genuine, like he knew something you didn’t but was just happy to leave it there for you to find out.
His dark hair was long and shaggy around his face; Mara had to strain to see the sharp edge of the jaw beneath it. But she wanted to. He wore glasses with thick black rims; they made his eyes seem large and innocent when he smiled up at her like this.
And now those eyes were watching her again, taking her in.

Prose movement
The guests’ arrival transformed the scene almost immediately, voices echoing through the corridors as they flowed from room to room, drawn by some invisible force to gather in the common area where Mara and Jonah stood. Among them was a young man who seemed as absorbed in his conversation as he was preoccupied with carrying his glass of water, moving through the group without a word or glance in either direction, focused entirely on reaching wherever he needed to go next. Mara watched him disappear behind a doorway into another room; his footsteps echoed away, then silence again.

segment:
After a second she dropped his hand, and they smiled awkwardly at each other. “Sorry. I’m Mara.”
“I know, I was just confirming that you didn’t get lost on the way over here. And that you haven’t already forgotten my name. But clearly you haven’t.” He said it lightly, as if he weren’t trying too hard. He was also a little taller than she had expected, and his dark blue eyes held an expression that made her look away again before she could see what it meant.
“I didn’t get lost,” she agreed. “And you’re Jonah.”
He shrugged. “Good so far.”
She took the first seat she found, near a fireplace that wasn’t lit.

“You can move if you want to,” he said.
“Is there another fire?” She looked around, half-joking. The room was mostly stone walls and wood floors with just enough furniture to keep it from looking like a prison cell.
